proof_skeleton_nl: Work with the set A_{m,g} of numerical semigroups of multiplicity m and genus g. Send a semigroup S in A_{m,g} to the tuple Phi(S) whose coordinate x_r records the first level q at which the residue class r modulo m enters S. Lemma L1 gives the residue-class threshold description, lemma L2 shows these thresholds satisfy the Kunz inequalities, and lemma L5 shows that their sum is exactly the genus. Hence Phi maps A_{m,g} into K_{m,g}. In the opposite direction, start from a tuple x in K_{m,g} and define Psi(x)=S_x by placing all multiples of m in the set and, in residue class r, including exactly the integers q m + r with q >= x_r. Lemma L3 proves that S_x is a numerical semigroup of multiplicity m. Lemma L4 shows that extracting thresholds from S_x recovers the original tuple x, and then lemma L5 gives genus(S_x)=x_1+...+x_{m-1}=g, so Psi maps K_{m,g} into A_{m,g}. The threshold characterization from L1 shows that reconstructing from Phi(S) recovers S exactly, while L4 shows that extracting thresholds from Psi(x) recovers x exactly. Thus Phi and Psi are inverse bijections between A_{m,g} and K_{m,g}. Taking cardinalities yields N(m,g)=|K_{m,g}|.

steps.derives: Fix integers m >= 2 and g >= 0. Let A = A_{m,g} be the set of numerical semigroups with multiplicity m and genus g, let B = K_{m,g}, let Phi : A -> tuples be the threshold extraction map described in shared context, and let Psi : B -> sets be the reconstruction map x |-> S_x.
steps.trivial_justification: This step only introduces the sets and maps that will be used in the proof.

steps.derives: For any S in A, the tuple x = Phi(S) is well-defined, each coordinate x_r is a positive integer, and for every r in {1,...,m-1} and every nonnegative integer q one has q m + r in S if and only if q >= x_r.
steps.trivial_justification: Apply L1 to the numerical semigroup S, using that S has multiplicity m because S belongs to A. This gives the exact threshold description of the nonzero residue classes of S modulo m.

steps.derives: For any S in A, the tuple x = Phi(S) satisfies all Kunz inequalities for multiplicity m.
steps.trivial_justification: Apply L2 to the same semigroup S and to the threshold tuple defined in A2. The conclusion is precisely the case-by-case Kunz system required in the definition of B.

steps.derives: For any S in A, if x = Phi(S), then x_1 + ... + x_{m-1} = g. Hence x belongs to B = K_{m,g}.
steps.trivial_justification: Because S belongs to A, its genus is g. Lemma L5 says that the genus of S equals the sum of the threshold coordinates x_r. Combining that equality with the positivity from A2 and the Kunz inequalities from A3 shows exactly that x satisfies every defining condition of K_{m,g}.

steps.derives: Phi is a well-defined function from A to B.
steps.trivial_justification: A4 established that every S in A is sent by Phi to an element of B.

steps.derives: For any x in B, the set Psi(x) = S_x is a numerical semigroup of multiplicity m.
steps.trivial_justification: An element x of B is, by definition, a positive tuple satisfying the Kunz inequalities. Applying L3 to that tuple yields that S_x is a numerical semigroup and that its multiplicity is m.

steps.derives: For any x in B and any r in {1,...,m-1}, the least positive integer q such that q m + r belongs to Psi(x) is exactly x_r.
steps.trivial_justification: This is exactly the content of L4 applied to the tuple x and the reconstructed set S_x = Psi(x).

steps.derives: For any x in B, the genus of Psi(x) is g. Therefore Psi(x) belongs to A.
steps.trivial_justification: By A7, the threshold tuple attached to the numerical semigroup Psi(x) is precisely x. Applying L5 to Psi(x) therefore gives genus(Psi(x)) = x_1 + ... + x_{m-1}. Since x belongs to B, that sum equals g. Together with A6, this shows Psi(x) is a numerical semigroup of multiplicity m and genus g, hence an element of A.

steps.derives: Psi is a well-defined function from B to A.
steps.trivial_justification: A8 established that every x in B is sent by Psi to an element of A.

steps.derives: For every S in A, Psi(Phi(S)) = S.
steps.trivial_justification: Let x = Phi(S). By A2, for each nonzero residue r modulo m, the elements of S in that residue class are exactly the numbers q m + r with q >= x_r. Also, because S is a numerical semigroup of multiplicity m, the element m belongs to S and closure under addition implies that every nonnegative multiple of m belongs to S. By definition, Psi(x) contains exactly those multiples of m and exactly those residue-class elements q m + r with q >= x_r. Therefore S and Psi(Phi(S)) have the same elements in every residue class modulo m, so they are equal.

steps.derives: For every x in B, Phi(Psi(x)) = x.
steps.trivial_justification: A7 says precisely that, after reconstructing Psi(x), the least positive q in residue class r is x_r for every r. Since Phi is defined by those least positive q values, Phi(Psi(x)) is exactly x.

steps.derives: The maps Phi : A -> B and Psi : B -> A are mutually inverse bijections. Consequently |A| = |B|.
steps.trivial_justification: A5 and A9 show that Phi and Psi are well-defined in opposite directions. A10 proves Psi o Phi is the identity on A, and A11 proves Phi o Psi is the identity on B. Therefore Phi is a bijection between A and B with inverse Psi. Bijections preserve cardinality, so |A| = |B|.

steps.derives: Since A is the set of numerical semigroups with multiplicity m and genus g, N(m,g) = |A| by definition; since B = K_{m,g}, A12 gives N(m,g) = |K_{m,g}|.
steps.trivial_justification: This is direct substitution of the definitions of A and B into the cardinality equality from A12.
